title: Section check: Stories, lives and public memory
intro: 10 questions about Lessons 11–15. Take your time. You can look back at the lessons and try again as often as you like.

questions.question: Each Vessantara panel shows a different episode. What is an episode?

options.text: The writing on a panel
options.feedback: Not quite. Writing on an object is an inscription. An episode is one part of a story. Look back at Lesson 11.

options.text: One part of a longer story
options.feedback: Yes. Chapter 2 and Chapter 3 show two episodes from the same story.

options.text: The wood the paint is on
options.feedback: Not quite. The panels are painted on teak wood. An episode is one part of a story. Look back at Lesson 11.

questions.question: The Thai panels have inscriptions that name donors. What do the inscriptions tell us?

options.text: Who asked for the panels to be made
options.feedback: Yes. Named donors asked for them, for religious reasons. We know this, even with no names for the painters.

options.text: The names of the painters who made them
options.feedback: Not quite. The museum has no names for the painters. The inscriptions name the donors. Look back at Lesson 11.

options.text: The year when the story first began
options.feedback: Not quite. The story is much older than the panels. The inscriptions name the donors. Look back at Lesson 11.

questions.question: The workers in The Harvesters are idealised. What does idealised mean?

options.text: Painted by the workers themselves
options.feedback: Not quite. Bruegel painted it for a rich trader. Idealised means shown as better than real life. Look back at Lesson 12.

options.text: Shown just as they really lived
options.feedback: Not quite. That is the opposite. Idealised means neater and more perfect than real life. Look back at Lesson 12.

options.text: Shown neater than in real life
options.feedback: Yes. The workers look neater and better than they did in real life. It is one view of farm life.

questions.question: Why did Millet begin to make prints like The Gleaners?

options.text: Partly to earn money and find buyers
options.feedback: Yes. Prints helped Millet reach buyers. Many of them were middle class.

options.text: To copy a painting by Bruegel
options.feedback: Not quite. Millet's print is his own work, made almost 300 years after Bruegel. Look back at Lesson 12.

options.text: Because a rich patron ordered just one
options.feedback: Not quite. A print is made in many copies for many buyers. Millet made prints partly to earn money. Look back at Lesson 12.

questions.question: What does Monet's painting of Argenteuil show in one picture?

options.text: A busy city street with no trees
options.feedback: Not quite. The painting shows a river path with trees and boats. Look back at Lesson 13.

options.text: Boats and trees, and factories far off
options.feedback: Yes. Fun on the river and factory chimneys share one scene. Nature and people's work are not split apart.

options.text: Farm workers cutting grain in a field
options.feedback: Not quite. That is The Harvesters. Argenteuil shows a river town near Paris. Look back at Lesson 13.

questions.question: In The Railway, a woman faces us and a girl looks through a fence. What can a careful viewer say?

options.text: What the two people are thinking
options.feedback: Not quite. The painting cannot show their thoughts. We can only guess. Look back at Lesson 13.

options.text: What they said to each other
options.feedback: Not quite. A painting cannot prove a conversation. It is easy to make one up. Look back at Lesson 13.

options.text: Where each person is looking
options.feedback: Yes. We can describe what we see, such as where they look. Their thoughts stay unknown.

questions.question: Rodin shows six citizens side by side, all on one level. What does this choice show?

options.text: One famous leader's victory
options.feedback: Not quite. The town first planned a monument to one man. Rodin showed all six instead. Look back at Lesson 14.

options.text: The power of England's king
options.feedback: Not quite. The king is not in the sculpture. It shows six citizens facing a hard choice. Look back at Lesson 14.

options.text: A shared act of courage
options.feedback: Yes. Showing all six made the monument about a shared act. Each man reacts in his own way.

stimulus.title: A made-up museum label
stimulus.body: This is a made-up example. Bronze statue of a sailor. It remembers a great storm in the year 1650. The artist made the model in 1900. This bronze cast was made from the model in 1990.

questions.question: When was this bronze statue itself made?

options.text: In 1990, when it was cast
options.feedback: Yes. The model came first. The bronze cast was made much later, in 1990.

options.text: In 1650, during the storm
options.feedback: Not quite. The storm is what the statue remembers. The bronze was made long after. Look back at Lesson 14.

options.text: In 1900, when the model was made
options.feedback: Not quite. The model was made in 1900. The bronze cast came later. Look back at Lesson 14.

questions.question: In Pieneman's painting, Dutch officers stand high under a raised flag. What does this choice do?

options.text: It shows how Diponegoro felt inside.
options.feedback: Not quite. A painted face or pose cannot prove what a person felt. Look back at Lesson 15.

options.text: It makes Dutch power look certain.
options.feedback: Yes. The painting was made for General De Kock. The tall officers and the flag make Dutch power look sure.

options.text: It questions the power of the Dutch.
options.feedback: Not quite. Saleh's later painting is the one scholars see as a challenge. Look back at Lesson 15.

stimulus.title: Two made-up paintings of one boat race
stimulus.body: This is a made-up example. A boat race took place in the made-up town of Pellam. The winning captain paid a painter to show the race. Years later, a second painter showed the same race from the losing crew's side.

questions.question: Which question is most useful to ask about the first painting?

options.text: Who paid for it, and why?
options.feedback: Yes. A commission matters. The captain paid for it, so it may show the race his way.

options.text: Is it bigger than the other one?
options.feedback: Not quite. Size does not tell you whose view it shows. Ask who it was made for. Look back at Lesson 15.

options.text: What colour is the captain's coat?
options.feedback: Not quite. That is a small detail. Ask who paid for it and why. Look back at Lesson 15.

results.high: Well done. You know a lot about how pictures and monuments tell stories and shape memory.
results.middle: Good work. You remember many of the main ideas. Look back at any lesson you want to check.
results.low: Thank you for trying. Look back at Lessons 11–15, then try again whenever you like.
